---
title: 'See builds on pull requests'
status: implemented
description: 'Oore reports each build to GitHub as a check run and to GitLab as a commit status, with links to the logs and installs.'
---

Every build of a GitHub or GitLab commit shows up on that commit, and so on
its pull request or merge request. Oore reports one check per platform the
build produces, for example `Release (Android)` and `Release (iOS)`.

## What you see

- **Queued** as soon as the build is created, so a push shows a pending check
  within a few seconds.
- **In progress** while a runner builds it.
- **Success**, **failure**, **timed out** or **cancelled** when it ends.

Each check links to the build in Oore. When a build succeeds with one
installable APK or IPA for that platform, the check links straight to its
install page instead. The GitHub check summary also lists every artifact
with an install link.

The check's name stays the pipeline and platform, so a required status check
in branch protection keeps matching.

## Steps

For a build that runs a version 2 [`.oore.yaml`](/reference/config/oore-yaml-v2),
the check shows the steps by the names the file gives them:

- The GitHub check summary names the workflow the pipeline builds, when it
  picks one, and ends with a table of the steps the runner ran, with each
  step's result and duration. The step that failed is in bold.
- When the build fails or times out, the check title, and on GitLab the
  status description, names the step it stopped at, for example
  `Build #12 failed at Run tests`.

Builds from a version 1 file or the pipeline form show the same check as
before, without steps.

## App size

When a build succeeds, the GitHub check summary also shows the size of each
artifact for that platform and how much it changed. Oore compares with the
latest earlier successful build of the same pipeline on the base branch: the
pull request's target branch, or the project's default branch for a push. A
build on the default branch therefore compares with the one before it. Builds
of the same commit are skipped, so a re-run never compares with itself.

Artifacts pair up by file name. When the name changes between builds, for
example because it carries a version, an artifact pairs with the only file of
the same kind in the baseline build, such as the only `.aab`. Split APKs pair
by name only. The build page shows the same comparison next to each artifact.

Oore records sizes when an upload finishes and keeps them after retention
deletes the files, so an old baseline still compares.

### Size budget

A pipeline can hold each kind of artifact to a size budget. Open the
pipeline's settings and add a rule under **Size budget** for a kind, named by
its file extension such as `aab`, `apk` or `ipa`. A rule sets any of:

- **Max size**: the largest the artifact may be.
- **Max increase**: how much it may grow compared with the baseline build
  above, in MB, in percent, or both.

Sizes are in binary units, like the rest of Oore: 1 MB is 1,048,576 bytes.
Every artifact of that kind on the check's platform must stay within all the
limits its rule sets. An artifact Oore cannot tie to a platform, such as a
`.zip`, counts against every check of the build. When the build has no
baseline, or an artifact has no match in it, only the max size applies, and
the summary says so. Any growth from a 0-byte baseline is over a percent
limit.

The budget's mode decides what an artifact over its budget does:

- **Fail the check**: the GitHub check concludes **failure**, its title says
  the build is over the size budget, and the summary lists each artifact,
  the limit it went over, and its size or change. On GitLab the commit status
  fails and its description names the first artifact and its change.
- **Warn**: the check keeps its result. The GitHub summary shows a warning
  with the same table, and the GitLab status description mentions it.

If Oore cannot load the sizes, the check keeps the build's result and its
summary says the size budget could not be checked.

Either way the build itself still succeeds, and its artifacts and releases are
unaffected. A required check that fails blocks merging like any other failed
check. The budget applies when a build reports its result, so a change to it
shows on the next build or re-run.

A re-run, or a second build of the same pipeline and commit, updates the
same check instead of adding another one. The newest build owns the check, so
an older build that finishes late does not overwrite it.

## What you need

- Your web UI's origin under **Allowed frontend origins** in **Settings >
  General > External access**, so the links point at it. Without one, checks
  still show their state but carry no links. People who open a link sign in
  as usual; the links do not grant access on their own.
- **GitHub:** the Oore GitHub App already asks for the `checks` permission.
  Nothing else to configure.
- **GitLab:** commit statuses need a credential with the `api` scope. A
  personal access token with only `read_api` still builds, but GitLab refuses
  the status and Oore skips it. An OAuth application source requests
  read-only scopes, so it does not report statuses. See
  [Connect GitLab](/build/sources/gitlab).

## Troubleshooting

**A build has no check on GitHub**

Open the GitHub App's installation settings and accept any pending
permission request, then re-run the build.

**A GitLab merge request has no status**

Replace the source's token with one that has the `api` scope.
